source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Indian Country west of the Mississippi (incl. Colorado plains and Front Range)
instrument_cite: 23rd Cong., Sess. I, Ch. 161, June 30, 1834 (as cited by source; 4 Stat. 729)
summary: The source argues the 1834 Act recognized Cheyenne title and required removal and fines of trespassers, but the US failed to enforce it for 39 years, and this non-enforcement was a major cause of Sand Creek. It says the Act was rescinded in 1873 after Homestead, Morrill and Pacific Railroad Acts of 1862 had dispersed Cheyenne land.
verbatim_quote: The federal government failed to deal with the illegal occupation, which lasted for 39 years, and the inaction caused measurable harm to the Cheyenne.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 1: 1834 Act text, Statute I, June 30, 1834
federal_account_contrast: Federal cession framing treats settlement as following lawful cession; source frames 1858-1861 Colorado settlement as illegal trespass under federal law the US itself refused to enforce.
map_implication: Add a layer/annotation: Colorado Front Range settlement 1858-1861 occurred on land that was Indian Country under the 1834 Act, before any cession.
notes: Claim that the Act was 'rescinded in 1873' is the author's and is not cited; verify. The 4 Stat. cite is reader-supplied.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: The source says 'treaty negotiations are a myth': commissioners arrived with prepared texts, read articles aloud, heard objections, and sent the unchanged text to the Senate, while Native leaders believed their spoken input was incorporated. Lakota speak of the 'Chicago Re-write' for 1868.
verbatim_quote: In every treaty we evaluated, the process was the same. Treaty commissioners represented the United States government; most often, these were military representatives who came with a prepared treaty in hand
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 3-5: DeMallie, Proceedings of the Great Peace Council 1867-68 (1975); Gary Roberts unpublished dissertation; Jefferson Davis quote
federal_account_contrast: Kappler presents treaty text as the negotiated agreement; the source says spoken terms the nations relied on were never written.
map_implication: In treaty detail panels, add a note that written text may not reflect what was agreed orally; link oral-term evidence where available.
notes: Generalization by the author across treaties evaluated.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Cheyenne governance: Council of Forty-Four Chiefs
summary: Cheyenne national decisions, especially war and peace and treaties, belonged to the Council of 44 (ten-year terms, equal band representation, consensus), with military societies (incl. Dog Men / Dog Soldiers) subordinate. This is the standard against which the source judges every treaty signature: individual chiefs acting without Council approval lacked authority.
verbatim_quote: The Council of Forty-Four Chiefs was a self-perpetuating body of tribal trustees; each member was selected by a predecessor
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 6-12: Sheldon Spotted Elk, 'Northern Cheyenne Tribe: Traditional Law and Constitutional Reform,' Tribal Law Journal 12 (2012); Leo Killsback, A Sacred People (2020) pp.27-28, 189; Grinnell, The Fighting Cheyennes pp.6-7
federal_account_contrast: Federal treaty records treat whoever marked a paper as authorized 'chiefs and headmen'; Cheyenne law required Council of 44 consent.
map_implication: Add a signatory-authority field to Cheyenne treaties: whether Council of 44 approval is documented.
notes: Lists ten bands incl. Hevhaitanio (Dog Men or Dog Soldiers) as a band and Hotametaneo'o (Dog Men) as a society. Source says bands may have last gathered as one around 1849, splitting North/South by 1857; others say they kept meeting incl. on Fort Laramie 1851 and Fort Wise 1861.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Confluence of Cheyenne River and Missouri River
instrument_cite: Not given in source (Kappler 2:232; 7 Stat. 255, July 6, 1825; reader-supplied, verify)
summary: First Cheyenne treaty. A Cheyenne representative took the proposal back to the Council of 44, which approved it; it allowed immigrants to cross Cheyenne territory undisturbed. With no Cheyenne interpreter, a Lakota gave the signers' names in Lakota, so the recorded names are Lakota renderings.
verbatim_quote: This treaty's unusual feature is that the Cheyenne names appear as Lakota names.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 13: author's own review of treaties
federal_account_contrast: Kappler lists names as if Cheyenne; source notes they are Lakota translations, a record-quality issue. Also a positive example where Council of 44 approval did occur.
map_implication: Note on the 1825 treaty: Council of 44 approval reported; signatory names are Lakota renderings.
notes: No land cession. Kappler/Stat. cite reader-supplied.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Platte River emigrant route
summary: From about 1845, and sharply after the 1849 California gold rush, emigrant trespass destroyed buffalo herds; this pressure produced the 1851 Fort Laramie council.
verbatim_quote: By 1849, the rush of illegal immigrants was destroying the buffalo herds.
sources_cited_by_source: None specific
federal_account_contrast: Federal framing treats emigrant trails as lawful passage; source calls emigrants illegal trespassers under the 1834 Act.
map_implication: Optional: show Platte emigrant route as pre-treaty trespass corridor.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Laramie / Horse Creek council grounds (approx. 42.20 N, -104.56 W for Fort Laramie)
instrument_cite: Not given in source (11 Stat. 749; Kappler 2:594; reader-supplied, verify)
summary: Commissioner D.D. Mitchell told the council the US did not want their land and that the boundaries were not intended to take land or limit hunting and passage; he promised compensation for 50 years, mainly for right of free passage on emigrant trails.
verbatim_quote: We do not come to you as traders ... We do not want your land, horses, robes, nor anything you have
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 14: Missouri Republican 1851 dispatches
federal_account_contrast: Later federal use of 1851 boundaries as the base for cessions and ICC claims contradicts the oral assurance that boundaries took no land.
map_implication: Render 1851 territory as a recognized homeland (not a cession), with Mitchell's assurance quoted.
notes: Mitchell also asked each tribe to designate a single chief.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Laramie
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Article 6 (head chiefs)
summary: Mitchell and Fitzpatrick wrongly believed the Cheyenne Medicine Chief could represent all Cheyenne; Article 6 bound nations to sustain US-selected 'head-chiefs'. The source says this subverted Council of 44 governance and set a precedent of holding whole tribes responsible for the acts of a few and of accepting signers who did not speak for the tribe.
verbatim_quote: Mitchell and Fitzpatrick made a serious error when they believed that the Medicine Chief of the Cheyenne could represent all of the Cheyenne in the treaty process.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text, Article 6
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text presents chosen head chiefs as national authority.
map_implication: Flag 1851 Cheyenne signatures as not representing the Council of 44.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Laramie
summary: The source lists possible Cheyenne signers (Stone Forehead of the Heviqsnipahis, chosen spokesman; Whiteface Bull, Oivimana; White Antelope, Isiometannui; Bear Feather, Wutapiu) and says all were Southerners representing only four of ten bands; no Northern band chief signed.
verbatim_quote: all the Chiefs who signed were Southerners, representing only four Manhao (what the Cheyenne called themselves) out of ten.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 27: Gary Roberts unpublished dissertation p.64

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Between the North Platte and Arkansas rivers (Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming)
summary: The US recognized the land between the North Platte and Arkansas as Cheyenne and Arapaho country. The source says assigning two sovereign nations one undivided tract violated their sovereignty and created later confusion; no Cheyenne-Arapaho line was drawn. Article 5 also preserved claims to other lands and hunting, fishing and passage rights.
verbatim_quote: the United States government recognized the land between the North Platte and Arkansas as the country of the Cheyenne and Arapaho.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty Article 5; endnote 16 (author note: 'Possible map showing the 1851 boundaries?')
federal_account_contrast: Atlas/Royce treat 1851 land as a starting tract later ceded; source stresses nothing was ceded in 1851.
map_implication: Draw 1851 Fort Laramie Cheyenne-Arapaho territory (North Platte to Arkansas, mountains to roughly the forks of the Republican/Smoky Hill per treaty text) as promised/recognized land, not ceded; note the treaty reserved rights to other lands.
notes: Source gives only North Platte-Arkansas; full metes and bounds are in treaty Article 5 (not reproduced in this chunk).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: 1851 treaty territories
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Article 5 final clause
summary: The source argues the reserved hunting, fishing and passage rights still exist unless a later treaty abrogated them, especially for Northern Cheyenne, many of whom say they never signed a treaty.
verbatim_quote: they do not surrender the privilege of hunting, fishing, or passing over any of the tracts of country heretofore described.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 17: Article 5 text
federal_account_contrast: Atlas cession polygons do not represent reserved usufructuary rights.
map_implication: Add 'reserved hunting/fishing/passage rights (claimed extant)' attribute to the 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho tract.
notes: Legal survival of rights is the author's argument.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho territory
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Articles 3 and 4
summary: Article 3 bound the US to protect the nations against depredations by US citizens, but set no enforcement method; the 1834 Act's removal and $500-$1,000 fines were never enforced. Article 4's phrase 'lawfully residing' conflicts with the 1834 Act, under which no settler could lawfully reside.
verbatim_quote: Such significant treaty violations were not enforced (or went unenforced), and this caused major economic harm for the Cheyenne.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 15: Sec. 11 of 1834 Act
federal_account_contrast: Adds treaty-protection violations not in a cession-only record.
map_implication: Record Article 3 non-enforcement as a violation of the 1851 treaty.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: Article 8 let the President withhold annuities from a whole nation for violations by any member, with no due process; the source calls it collective punishment and says the government did later manipulate annuities.
verbatim_quote: The government could manipulate annuities, and they did.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text
map_implication: Note annuity-withholding clause in 1851 treaty record.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
nations: Cheyenne; Arapaho; Lakota; Crow; Plains nations
instrument_cite: Prucha, American Indian Treaties pp.440-442; Kappler vol. IV p.1078-1080 (as cited)
summary: The Senate unilaterally cut annuities from 50 years to 10 (plus 5 at the President's discretion). Only three nations' assent was obtained; an Indian Office endorsement says the Indians 'never got together for the purpose'. Only four of six original Cheyenne signers and two of three Arapaho appear on the amendment. The treaty was omitted from Statutes at Large in 1867 and never proclaimed.
verbatim_quote: This [amendment] was to be submitted to the Indians, but they never got together for the purpose.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 18-23: Prucha pp.440-442; Luke Lea to A.H.H. Stuart May 29, 1852 (Kappler IV:1078); Harry Anderson, Nebraska History 37 (1956); Kappler IV:1080
federal_account_contrast: Kappler 1904 printed the treaty as amended and accepted; Kappler later (1929) admitted the error. Royce 1899 p.786 footnote says the treaty was never ratified.
map_implication: Mark Fort Laramie 1851 as Senate-amended without full consent and never proclaimed; show that Kappler vol. II text is misleading on assent.
notes: Source contains date errors: says Senate 'ratified' Sept 17, 1851 (actually the signing date) and that the treaty went to Fillmore Feb 17, 1852 and he refused to sign; Senate struck 50-year term May 24 (1852). Verify against Prucha.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Washington DC
instrument: Commissioner Luke Lea to Secretary A.H.H. Stuart, May 29, 1852
instrument_cite: Kappler vol. IV p.1078 (as cited)
summary: The Commissioner of Indian Affairs himself wrote that a treaty amended without Indian consent is a 'mockery' of contract. A federal official's own admission useful for the atlas.
verbatim_quote: how such a proceeding in view of the legal principles involved, can be considered anything but a mockery of the highest and most solemn form of contract it is difficult to perceive.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 2 and 19: Kappler IV:1078; Prucha p.440
federal_account_contrast: Primary federal source contradicting unilateral amendment practice.
map_implication: Quote in the 'Senate amended without consent' category explainer.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Roy v. United States and Oglala and Cheyenne Indians (Ct. Cl. 1910); Moore v. United States and the Sioux and Cheyenne (1897)
instrument_cite: Cited via Prucha p.442 n.; also New York Indians v. US, 170 U.S. 1 (source prints '170, U.S. 23')
summary: The Court of Claims held presidential proclamation unnecessary and treated the 1851 treaty as valid, reasoning from a 'wards' fiduciary theory and claiming the Sioux agreed to the amendment. The source disputes the factual premise and the diminished-sovereignty reasoning. In the 1920s Secretary of State Kellogg refused to have the President proclaim it.
verbatim_quote: The Indians were our wards, and we thus occupied a fiduciary relationship to them.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 24: Prucha pp.441-442
federal_account_contrast: Shows federal branches disagreed on whether the 1851 treaty was ever in force.
map_implication: Ratification-status field for 1851 should read 'contested: never proclaimed; Court of Claims treated as valid'.
notes: Source names 'Francis Kellogg' (Frank B. Kellogg). New York Indians cite as printed appears wrong; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)

sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 26: Prucha p.441

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)

summary: Cheyenne warriors killed and scalped a Shoshone father and son traveling to the council; the Cheyenne chiefs then held a 'scalp peace', returning undanced scalps with gifts. The Missouri Republican also describes the military societies as able to act without chiefs' consent.
verbatim_quote: They are so numerous and so well banded together that the chiefs can do nothing with them.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 28: Missouri Republican 1851 (A.B. Chambers, B. Gratz Brown)
federal_account_contrast: Not in treaty record.

sources_cited_by_source: Act text quoted

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)

summary: Grattan fired on Brule Sioux in the 1854 'Mormon cow' affair, killing Conquering Bear, whom the source says was coerced into signing the 1851 treaty as Lakota representative. Afterward the US military struck a Cheyenne camp and killed ten people; Cheyenne retaliation killed 18 whites.
verbatim_quote: the United States military struck the Cheyenne camp and killed ten people.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 29: Nadeau, Fort Laramie and the Sioux Indians pp.90-91; Hafen and Young, Fort Laramie and the Pageant of the West pp.221-245

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Solomon's Fork (Kansas)
summary: War Department ordered a punitive expedition against the Cheyenne eight days after agent Twiss concluded a peace, for acts already 'settled and forgiven by treaty'. Col. Sumner's 1857 campaign defeated the Cheyenne; Northern bands withdrew to the Powder River and Southern bands were left in the path of expansion.
verbatim_quote: The punishment to be administered was for the activities occurring in the preceding two years (previously settled and forgiven by treaty).
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 31-32: Chalfant, Cheyennes and Horse Soldiers pp.59-61; Grinnell, The Fighting Cheyenne pp.112-123
federal_account_contrast: Battle of Solomon's Fork is usually framed as a military victory, not punishment for settled grievances.
map_implication: Add Solomon's Fork 1857 as violence event preceding the gold rush and Fort Wise.
notes: Not described as a massacre by source; categorized as mass violence.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Bent's Fort
summary: High Back Wolf, Sweet Medicine Chief, led Council chiefs (White Antelope, Tall Bull, Lean Bear) to Bent's Fort, saying they had honored Fort Laramie; they would accept a new treaty only if they could keep their lands.
verbatim_quote: The Southern leaders were agreeable to a new treaty as long as they could keep their lands
sources_cited_by_source: None specific

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Colorado Front Range; Denver; gold districts
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851; Trade and Intercourse Act 1834
summary: Up to 100,000 gold seekers entered the Front Range in three years, all trespassers under the 1851 treaty and the 1834 Act; instead of removing them, Commissioner A.B. Greenwood and others worked to relocate the Cheyenne and Arapaho to a small desolate tract in southeastern Colorado.
verbatim_quote: Every one of these individuals was illegally intruding on Indian land.
sources_cited_by_source: None specific
federal_account_contrast: Royce dates the Colorado taking from the 1861 cession; the occupation and town-building began in 1858 without any cession.
map_implication: Show 1858-1861 Front Range settlement as illegal occupation predating any cession.
notes: 100,000 figure is an estimate without cite.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: The US created separate northern and southern agencies, fostering the 'flawed notion' that the two groups were politically independent; the Southern chiefs refused to make a separate peace without their Northern relatives.
verbatim_quote: The Southern Chiefs had spoken but would not propose a separate peace without regard to their Northern relatives.
federal_account_contrast: Federal records treat Northern and Southern Cheyenne as distinct parties.
map_implication: Do not split Cheyenne polygons into Northern/Southern ownership before 1861 without explanation.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Wise (later Fort Lyon), Arkansas River, Colorado
instrument_cite: Not given in source (12 Stat. 1163; Kappler 2:807; reader-supplied, verify)
summary: On learning of Greenwood's proposal, the Cheyenne convened the Council of 44, which with the societies decided not to attend and to give up no land. Greenwood replied he would make the treaty 'over the heads of the Cheyenne'. Northern leaders refused; the chiefs said Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho must be asked or negotiate their own treaty.
verbatim_quote: We will make this Treaty over the Heads of the Cheyenne.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 33-36: Margaret Coel, Chief Left Hand (1981) pp.110-122, 114, 120
federal_account_contrast: Kappler presents Fort Wise as a treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho of the Upper Arkansas 'duly authorized'; the Council of 44 had formally refused.
map_implication: Flag Royce 477 (Fort Wise cession) as made against an explicit Council of 44 refusal.
notes: Greenwood quote is via Coel p.120.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Wise, Colorado (Bent's New Fort area, approx. 38.07 N, -103.18 W; approximate)
summary: Agent A.G. Boone 'randomly appointed six Indians' to sign. Black Kettle and White Antelope attended without Council of 44 permission and two years later denied signing. Listed Cheyenne signers: Black Kettle, White Antelope, Lean Bear, Little Wolf, Tall Bear, Left Hand (Namos); Arapaho: Little Raven, Storm, Shaved Head, Big Mouth.
verbatim_quote: They were there without the permission of the Council of 44 and had no official authority to sign or approve any documents.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)

Only one signature was ever obtained, from a drunk non-leader. The source concludes land north of the South Platte was never ceded by the Northern people and was taken illegally.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Denver City and adjacent towns
instrument_cite: State Dept letter Aug 12, 1861 (endnote 48)
summary: Article 11 would have let Denver citizens enter town land at $1.25 an acre 'in consideration of the kind treatment' by Denver citizens. The Senate struck it unilaterally in executive session; State then directed Dole to get the original signers' assent.
verbatim_quote: In consideration of the kind treatment of the Arapaho and Cheyenne by the citizens of Denver City and adjacent towns
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 47-48: Rocky Mountain News Apr 18, 1860; State Dept letter Aug 12, 1861
federal_account_contrast: Kappler shows the treaty as amended and assented.
map_implication: Mark Fort Wise as Senate-amended (Art. 11 stricken) with disputed assent.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Left Hand's camp, Denver
summary: While Left Hand's warriors were away, drunken white men led by Charles Gardner ('Big Phil the Cannibal') invaded the lodges and raped women and girls; Denver authorities knew who did it and did nothing.
verbatim_quote: Even though Denver authorities and leaders knew who had committed this heinous crime, NOTHING was done to this gang of rapists.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 47: Rocky Mountain News, April 18, 1860
federal_account_contrast: Contradicts the 'kind treatment' recital in Fort Wise Article 11.
map_implication: Add as a mass-violence event at Denver, 1860.
notes: Sexual violence; not a killing massacre. Categorized under MASSACRE as mass violence.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Wise
instrument: Fort Wise amendment assent, dated October 29, 1861
instrument_cite: Original handwritten treaty and amendment (endnotes 50, 52)
summary: The October 29 amendment assent shows erased and replaced dates, signers in the same order as February, and '+' marks apparently by one hand rather than individual X marks. The State Department letter says the Senate ratified Aug 6, 1861 with an amendment already 'assented to', before the tribes gathered. The source calls this circumstantial and its own view speculative.
verbatim_quote: The amendment to the Treaty dated October 29 has plus (+) marks, not X's, and they all appear to be made by the same person, not by each individual signer.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 50-55: original manuscripts; Rocky Mountain News Sept 11, 1861; transmittal letter in amendment
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows valid assent in 'full council' Oct 29, 1861 (per document found by Gary Roberts).
map_implication: Flag Fort Wise amendment assent as possibly forged; needs document examination.
notes: Author explicitly says 'My opinion is speculative and based on circumstantial evidence.' Gary Roberts found a document saying chiefs approved amendment 'in full council' Oct 29, 1861.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Wise / Fort Lyon
summary: Governor Gilpin had Boone withhold annuities all summer; about 3,000 hungry Indians gathered demanding them. Per Thom Hatch via Gary Roberts, Boone got the amendment signed by promising 36 military uniforms (six with epaulets) and a Washington trip, though Black Kettle had said he would never sign another treaty.
verbatim_quote: Many of them were suffering from hunger, and the commanding officer had already distributed some provisions among them.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 49, 51: Gary Roberts correspondence Sept 14, 2023; Rocky Mountain News 9/11/1861; Thom Hatch, Black Kettle biography
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows voluntary assent.
map_implication: Flag Royce 477 / Fort Wise amendment as obtained under starvation duress and inducements.
notes: Quote is from Rocky Mountain News as reprinted.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Sand Creek reserve; Smoky Hill country
summary: Gary Roberts writes that Black Kettle believed Fort Wise bound only the bands party to it, not Northerners or absent Southerners (most of whom were on the Solomon and Republican), and that he saw the Sand Creek reservation as a safe haven. He was infuriated when Governor Evans claimed it applied to all Cheyenne, and in 1863 refused towns along a Smoky Hill railroad route.
verbatim_quote: It is clear that Black Kettle believed that the treaty of Fort Wise applied only to the manhao who were parties to the treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 49: Gary Roberts correspondence Sept 14, 2023; Thom Hatch
federal_account_contrast: Evans and later federal practice applied Fort Wise to all Cheyenne.
map_implication: Draw the Fort Wise (Sand Creek) reservation as land promised and later taken; note Black Kettle's scope understanding.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Wise reservation, southeastern Colorado ('no-water land')
summary: The promised reservation, which the Southern Arapaho called 'no-water land', overlapped land the War Department had already taken as a 25-mile military reserve. The source says the treaty traded the best hunting grounds and 53 million acres for a small, bone-dry reservation.
verbatim_quote: The Treaty had them giving up their best hunting grounds and 53 million acres of land for a small, desolate, bone-dry reservation.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 33: Coel pp.110-122
federal_account_contrast: Treaty reservation shown as a clean grant; part was already military reserve.
map_implication: Draw the Fort Wise reservation (Sand Creek reserve) as promised land, overlapped by Fort Wise/Lyon military reserve.
notes: Reservation boundaries not given in this chunk; take from treaty Article 1 text. 53 million acre figure uncited.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Mouth of the Huerfano River, Colorado (Boone ranch)
summary: Dr. F.B. Culver, hired to manage gifts, won $5,000 'out of Indian money' in the Court of Claims on what the source calls a fraudulent claim. Agent A.G. Boone was building a ranch on Indian land at the mouth of the Huerfano River, an undisclosed conflict of interest. Dole appointed his cousin Samuel G. Colley to Boone's post.
verbatim_quote: He was awarded $5,000 out of Indian money for his fraudulent claim.
sources_cited_by_source: None specific
map_implication: Add fraud notes to Fort Wise record.
notes: Uncited. Source spells Colley as 'Cooley' in one place.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Denver: 960-acre (1 by 1.5 mile) rectangle covering Auraria and Denver City plats
instrument: Act of May 28, 1864 'for the relief of the citizens of Denver' (Congressional Grant)
instrument_cite: Not given in source (13 Stat. 94; reader-supplied, verify)
summary: Denver's town companies sold lots from 1858 with no title, on land Smiley (History of Denver, 1901) called Indian land not open to entry. Congress confirmed their titles by the 1864 Congressional Grant; the source says the tribes were never compensated and the transfer should be voided.
verbatim_quote: All of them were merely squatters on land to which the Indians had the first claim under the conditions then existing.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 57-59: Jerome Smiley, History of Denver (1901)
federal_account_contrast: Royce/atlas would show Denver within the 1861 cession; source shows title came from an 1864 statute on land the Northern bands never ceded.
map_implication: Add a Denver 1864 Congressional Grant polygon (960 acres) flagged 'title by statute on uncompensated, contested land'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Colorado
instrument: Homestead Act, Pacific Railroad Act, Morrill Act (1862)
summary: These Acts moved unceded Indian land into the public domain; the Pacific Railroad Act gave a 200-foot right-of-way and 6,400 acres per mile. Governor Evans sat on a railroad commission board.
verbatim_quote: In 1862, the Homestead Act, the Pacific Railroad Act, and the Morrill Act all transferred vast areas of stolen Indian land into the public domain.
map_implication: Cross-reference railroad and Morrill grants on Cheyenne-Arapaho land north of the South Platte.
notes: 6,400 acres per mile matches the 1864 amended grant; 1862 grant was 10 sections (6,400 acres) per mile on both sides. Verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Land north and west of the South Platte, incl. Denver and Front Range mining districts
instrument: Opinion of U.S. Attorney S.E. Browne, Denver, 1863
instrument_cite: Via Unrau, 'Prelude to War' (1964)
summary: U.S. Attorney S.E. Browne, after the Interior Secretary did not answer his query, opined that land north and west of the South Platte had not been ceded and that Denver and the gold districts were occupied by trespassers. Evans rejected it; Dole, fearing the Northerners would win in court, ordered Evans to hold another council and get the remaining chiefs to sign.
verbatim_quote: The land north and west of the South Platte had not been ceded.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 61: Unrau, 'Prelude to War,' Colorado Magazine 1964
federal_account_contrast: A federal law officer contemporaneously concluded the land was unceded.
map_implication: Strong basis to mark land north/west of South Platte as NEVER_CEDED (1861-1868), citing Browne 1863 and Unrau 1964.
notes: Dole quote: go 'ahead with another council and get the rest of the chiefs to agree to the treaty of 1861.'

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Colorado Territory
instrument: Dole to Evans, July 16, 1863; Charles E. Mix directive, 1864
summary: Evans ignored Dole's order to hold a council and rejected peace-seeking leaders. The Indian Office (acting Commissioner Charles E. Mix) rejected his plan to separate 'friendly' from 'hostile' Indians and directed him to keep the peace and concentrate Indians near the buffalo range, not on reservations.
verbatim_quote: It is not contemplated that the Indians should be collected and fed on the reservations, but they should be concentrated, if anywhere, about the buffalo range.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 62-63: Dole to Evans July 16, 1863
federal_account_contrast: Shows Evans acted against his own superiors' orders.
map_implication: Attach to Sand Creek event: Evans acted contrary to Indian Office direction.
notes: Endnote 63 misplaced (says it is the first proclamation date).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Colorado plains; Fort Lyon rendezvous
instrument: Governor John Evans proclamations of June 27, 1864 and August 11, 1864
instrument_cite: Endnotes 63-64
summary: Evans's first proclamation effectively declared war on Indians not at Fort Lyon; the second authorized all Colorado citizens to pursue, kill and destroy 'hostile Indians' and keep their property. The source says the second led directly to Sand Creek, on homelands the people had not surrendered.
verbatim_quote: to kill and destroy as enemies of the country wherever they may be found, all such hostile Indians.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 63-64
federal_account_contrast: Territorial authorization of private killing on unceded land.
map_implication: Add Evans proclamations as events tied to the Sand Creek massacre and to Royce 477 land.
notes: The sentence 'As a reward for killing these Indians, you have permission to keep the property of the victims' is presented inside the quote but reads as paraphrase; the original says citizens may hold captured property. Verify wording.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Sand Creek, Kiowa County, Colorado (approx. 38.55 N, -102.51 W, Sand Creek Massacre NHS)
instrument_cite: Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War (1865); Joint Special Committee on the Condition of the Indian Tribes (1865/1867)
summary: The source does not retell the massacre but holds Governor Evans more responsible than anyone, saying he rejected peace offers and was never indicted. The Joint Committee found Chivington 'surprised and murdered, in cold blood' people who believed they were under US protection, and called for Evans's removal; Chivington resigned and was never prosecuted.
verbatim_quote: surprised and murdered, in cold blood, the unsuspecting men, women, and children on Sand Creek, who had every reason to believe they were under the protection of the United States authorities
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes 1-7: Gary Roberts, Massacre at Sand Creek; John M. Carroll ed., The Sand Creek Massacre: A Documentary History (1973); congressional reports (endnotes in next chunk)
federal_account_contrast: Atlas cession record does not tie Royce 477 to the massacre on the promised reservation.
map_implication: Mark Sand Creek massacre on the Fort Wise reservation; link to Fort Wise and Evans proclamations; note it preceded the 1865 Little Arkansas treaty.
notes: Part II endnotes fall outside this chunk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: Colorado Delegate Allen A. Bradford charged Evans with a policy that provoked hostility and with having 'given countenance and encouragement to the massacre of peaceable Indians'. Evans later regained standing and has streets, towns and a mountain named for him.
verbatim_quote: He had given countenance and encouragement to the massacre of peaceable Indians and destroyed their faith and confidence in the sincerity and obligation of government treaties.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnote 3 (in next chunk)
map_implication: Place-name layer: flag Mount Evans-type names (now Mount Blue Sky) tied to Evans.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Near Gillette's Ranch; Julesburg, Colorado area
summary: Eugene Ware records a strychnine-poisoned whiskey barrel left for Indians near Gillette's Ranch; Tall Bull family oral history and other oral accounts say settlers poisoned hungry Cheyenne with strychnine, including around Julesburg.
verbatim_quote: they put a lot of strychnine in a barrel of whiskey and stuck it up where Indians could get it.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 65-66: Eugene F. Ware, The Indian War of 1864 p.378; family stories of Ritch and Bill Tall Bull; Part II endnote 10
federal_account_contrast: Absent from federal record.
map_implication: Add poisoning reports as oral-history violence events near Julesburg; mark evidence level oral/second-hand.
notes: Ware's account is hearsay from a soldier.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
summary: The source calls the Peace Commission a pretense to confine Indians or eliminate them; its final resolutions sought transfer to the War Department and an end to treaty-making. Sherman and Grant statements (NYT Oct 16, 1868) endorse extermination if necessary. A Denver crowd (Doolittle visit) shouted 'Exterminate them!'
verbatim_quote: General Grant told the same reporter that the settlers and emigrants had to be protected even if it meant the extermination of every Indian Tribe.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnotes 67-71: DeMallie/Deloria, Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission (1975); Utley, The Indian Frontier pp.102, 125; New York Times Oct 16, 1868
map_implication: Context for 1867-68 treaties signed under explicit extermination threat.
notes: Source attributes 'only good Indian' quote to Sheridan without cite.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
nations: Cheyenne; Arapaho; Oglala and Sicangu Lakota
place: Julesburg, Colorado; Mud Springs and Rush Creek, Nebraska
summary: After Sand Creek all the chiefs pledged war and sent the pipe; the source says this was the only time the Cheyenne ever declared war on the intruders (late 1864 to 1879). Black Kettle and about 80 lodges went south of the Arkansas instead.
verbatim_quote: This was the only time the Cheyenne ever declared war against the intruders.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes 8-16 (author's grandmother; others in next chunk)
federal_account_contrast: Federal accounts frame 1865 raids as aggression rather than a declared response to a massacre.
map_implication: Context only.
notes: Source date 'February 2, 1862' for leaving the South Platte camp is an error for 1865.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Black Bear's camp, Wolf Creek / Tongue River (Wyoming)
summary: Gen. Patrick Connor ordered officers to refuse peace overtures and 'kill every male Indian over 12'; superiors countermanded it but killing continued. Troops attacked Black Bear's Arapaho camp while men were away, destroying it; Pawnee scouts killed 24 Cheyenne.
verbatim_quote: You will not receive overtures of peace or submission from Indians but will attack and kill every male Indian over 12 years of age.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes 19-21 (next chunk)
federal_account_contrast: Usually called the Battle of the Tongue River (Connor Battle).
map_implication: Add Black Bear camp attack (Connor Battle site, Ranchester WY) as violence event on 1851-recognized land; add Pawnee-scout killing of 24 Cheyenne.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Laramie, Dakota Territory
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie with the Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868
instrument_cite: Not given (15 Stat. 655; Kappler 2:1012; reader-supplied, verify)
summary: Only four Council of 44 chiefs (Little Wolf, Dull Knife, Big Wolf, Short Hair) signed; other Northern chiefs disagreed and were angry with Little Wolf, and most Northern people rejected it because the Council of 44 did not approve it. Many Northern Cheyenne say they never signed a treaty.
verbatim_quote: Most Northern People rejected the 1868 Treaty as a binding agreement because the Council of 44 did not approve it.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes 36-37 (next chunk; Peter Powell cited in text)
federal_account_contrast: Treaty says signers were 'duly authorized to act in the premises'.
map_implication: Flag the 1868 Northern Cheyenne-Arapaho cession as signed without Council of 44 approval; consider NEVER_CEDED/contested for Northern Cheyenne lands.
notes: Signature list shows 14 x-marks with Sorrel Horse twice.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Black Hills; Powder River; from North Platte to the Yellowstone; west to the Big Horns, east to the Missouri
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1868 (Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho)
summary: Signers were told negotiators acknowledged their claims to the Black Hills and country from the North Platte to the Yellowstone; per Peter Powell, Little Wolf was told a great swath north of the Platte, west to the Big Horns and east to the Missouri, would belong to the Cheyenne and Arapaho. The written text required Lakota permission.
verbatim_quote: Little Wolf was told by the commissioners that a great swath of land north of the Platte River and stretching west to the Big Horns and east to the Missouri would belong to the Cheyenne and Arapaho.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnote 36 (next chunk); Peter Powell
federal_account_contrast: Written treaty gives no reservation of their own; oral promise of a large territory.
map_implication: Draw an 'orally promised 1868 Cheyenne-Arapaho territory' (North Platte to Yellowstone, Big Horns to Missouri) as contested promised land.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Medicine Lodge (Southern C&A) reservation; Great Sioux Reservation; Crow agency near Otter Creek
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1868 (Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho), Article 2
summary: Article 2 ceded all territory outside the Medicine Lodge Southern Cheyenne-Arapaho reservation or the 1868 Sioux reservation, keeping the right to hunt while game lasted. The source says those placements never happened, so Article 2 failed and the treaty is void absent a mutual amendment; the Northern Cheyenne reservation was later created by executive order outside the treaty's terms.
verbatim_quote: The creation of the two proposed reservations never happened, rendering Article 2 invalid and thereby voiding the treaty
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text, Article 2
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats the 1868 cession as complete.
map_implication: Mark the 1868 Northern Cheyenne cession as conditional on a reservation never provided; show the Northern Cheyenne reservation as executive-order land, not a treaty reservation.
notes: Legal conclusion is the author's.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1868 (NC & NA), Article 8; Agreement of 1876 ratified Feb 28, 1877
instrument_cite: Act of Feb 28, 1877, ch. 72 (44th Cong., 2d Sess.) (19 Stat. 254, reader-supplied)
summary: Article 8 required any cession to be signed by a majority of adult males. The source says the 1876-77 Manypenny agreement, which ceded Black Hills land and all outside the reduced Sioux reservation incl. hunting rights, could not have been signed by Cheyenne already removed to Oklahoma and lacked majority assent.
verbatim_quote: No treaty for the cession ... shall be of any force or validity as against the said Indians unless executed and signed by at least a majority of all the adult male Indians
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty Art. 8; 1877 Act text
federal_account_contrast: Act states the Northern Arapaho and Cheyenne were 'duly authorized' parties.
map_implication: Flag 1877 Black Hills cession as lacking Article 8 majority for Northern Cheyenne.
notes: Source's chronology is wrong: it dates the agreement September 1877 (text says Spotted Tail Agency, September 28, 1877), but the agreement was signed Sept-Oct 1876 and ratified Feb 28, 1877, before the May 1877 removal. The 'could not have signed' argument needs re-checking; the majority-consent argument stands independently.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
nations: Sioux bands; Northern Arapaho; Northern Cheyenne
place: Great Sioux Reservation western boundary: 103rd meridian, South and North Forks Cheyenne River, Cannon Ball River
instrument: Agreement of 1876 (Manypenny Commission), ratified Act of Feb 28, 1877, Articles 1-5
instrument_cite: 44th Cong. 2d Sess. ch. 72
summary: Article 1 redrew the western/northern boundaries along the 103rd meridian, the forks of the Cheyenne River and the Cannon Ball River, ceding all outside including hunting rights and abrogating Art. 16 of the 1868 Sioux treaty. Article 4 pushed removal to Indian Territory; Article 5 tied rations to school attendance.
verbatim_quote: the said Indians do hereby relinquish and cede to the United States all the territory lying outside the said reservation, as herein modified and described, including all privileges of hunting
sources_cited_by_source: Act text; endnotes 54-57 (next chunk)
federal_account_contrast: Rations-for-cession ('sign or starve') context is not in the source here.
map_implication: Ensure Northern Cheyenne are listed as parties affected by the 1877 Black Hills taking polygon; boundary description usable for mapping.
notes: Commissioners included A.G. Boone of Fort Wise.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Red Fork of the Powder River (Willow Creek), about 20 miles west of Kaycee, Wyoming
summary: US troops found and burned the 173-lodge Northern Cheyenne village, destroying winter supplies; the source says it affected the Cheyenne more than Little Bighorn. Starvation forced surrenders in spring 1877.
verbatim_quote: U.S. troops found them and burned their village.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes 44-46 (next chunk)
federal_account_contrast: Usually framed as a battle (Dull Knife Fight).
map_implication: Add Dull Knife Fight (Red Fork Powder River) as violence event leading to surrender and removal.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Fort Robinson, Nebraska to Darlington Agency, Indian Territory (Oklahoma)
summary: After surrendering (Dull Knife and Standing Elk April 21, 1877; Little Wolf with 386), about 936 Northern Cheyenne (117 lodges) were forcibly moved to the Southern Cheyenne (Darlington) agency despite a promise they could stay north. Agent Miles withheld rations as punishment; nearly 50 died of disease and starvation.
verbatim_quote: The Cheyenne were promised that they could stay in the north, but on May 29, the Cheyenne were removed to the Darlington Agency in Oklahoma.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes 47-53 (next chunk)
map_implication: Draw 1877 removal route Fort Robinson to Darlington; flag broken promise to remain north.
notes: Source gives both May 28 and May 29.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024, The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes, Cheyenne History (Part I 1825-1864; Part II 1864-1879)
place: Rosebud; Little Bighorn (Montana)
summary: Cheyenne accounts of the Little Bighorn were discounted because they used different cardinal directions; Richard Fox's 1984-85 archaeology found the Cheyenne accounts most accurate. Rosebud is the battle 'where the girl saved her brother' (Buffalo Calf Road Woman). Context: 1874 refusal to sell the Black Hills.
verbatim_quote: when the correct cardinal directions as used by the Cheyenne were applied to the battlefield site, the Cheyenne stories were the most accurate.
sources_cited_by_source: Part II endnotes 38-43 (next chunk)
federal_account_contrast: Validates Cheyenne oral history over military accounts.
map_implication: Context only.
